rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threatened punishment answers the Meccans’ public taunts against Islam and hidden plotting; the Prophet is to leave its timing to God because he cannot measure their guilt or know whether the term is near or far.
rows.anchor: منشأ توجه العذاب إليهم هو ما كانوا يطعنون به في الإسلام في الظاهر وما يبطنون من المكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The public words are the polytheists’ mockery and attacks on Islam, while what they conceal is their plot and deception against it.
rows.anchor: المراد بالجهر من القول ما أظهره المشركون من القول في الإسلام طعنا واستهزاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “perhaps it” is said to refer to an unmentioned thing, perhaps the commanded notification: God may use the warning to test them, expose their inner stance, and grant respite until a term.
rows.anchor: وضمير { لعله } على ما قيل كناية عن غير مذكور ولعله راجع إلى الإيذان المأمور به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “He said” refers to the Prophet; after they reject his message, he turns to God asking Him to judge by the truth and make it manifest for and against whoever deserves it.
rows.anchor: الضمير في { قال } للنبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم والآية حكاية قول النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the judgment “by the truth” is explanatory, not restrictive, since every divine judgment is true.
rows.anchor: وتقييد الحكم بالحق توضيحي لا احترازي فإن حكمه تعالى لا يكون إلا حقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet then addresses the opponents: God is Lord of both sides, merciful to the one who turns to Him, and the unfailing helper who establishes truth against their false claims about the religion.
rows.anchor: فهو سبحانه ربه وربهم جميعا فله أن يحكم بين مربوبيه، وهو كثير الرحمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “What you describe” means their false characterization of their religion and their slanderous attacks on the true religion.
rows.anchor: وهو نعتهم دينهم بما ليس فيه وطعنهم في الدين الحق بما هو بريء من ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse’s rhetorical features include a shift from direct address to third person, then a shift from “my Lord” to “our Lord,” and the names “the Merciful” and “the One invoked for help.”
rows.anchor: كالالتفات من الخطاب إلى الغيبة في { قال } والتعبير عنه تعالى أولا بربي وثانيا بربنا

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Muhammad ibn Muslim reports from Abu Jaʿfar that every town God destroys with punishment does not return.
rows.anchor: كل قرية أهلكها الله بعذاب فإنهم لا يرجعون

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: In a report from Abu Jaʿfar through Abu al-Jarud, Meccan opponents challenge the verse about worshipped objects as fuel for Hell; Ibn al-Zibara argues that Jesus, his mother, and angels would then be included, but the Prophet answers that God has already exempted those promised good, quoting 21:101–102.
rows.anchor: لما نزلت هذه الآية يعني قوله { إنكم وما تعبدون من دون الله حصب جهنم } وجد منها أهل مكة وجدا شديدا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: An alternate account says Ibn al-Zibara applies the warning to every object worshipped, then cites Jesus, Uzayr, and angels; the Prophet agrees they were righteous, and the crowd rejoices before the exemption is revealed.
rows.anchor: ألست تزعم يا محمد أن عيسى عبد صالح وأن عزير عبد صالح وأن الملائكة صالحون؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Ibn ʿAbbās version is historically flawed: Uzayr is named in a late Medinan sura, not in the Meccan suras.
rows.anchor: ذكر اسم عزير والواقعة في أوائل البعثة بمكة ولم يذكر اسمه في شيء من السور المكية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story wrongly says Jews worshipped Uzayr; they called him God’s son as an honorific.
rows.anchor: واليهود لا تعبد عزيرا وإنما قالوا عزير ابن الله تشريفا كما قالوا نحن أبناء الله وأحباؤه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story’s claim that the exemption was revealed only after the Prophet conceded the verse’s universal scope delays clarification past the time of need and strengthens the accusation against him.
rows.anchor: وهذا من ورود البيان بعد وقت الحاجة وأشد تأييدا لوقوع التهمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account’s assertion that 43:57 was revealed during this incident is also implausible because that verse has no connection to the story’s content.
rows.anchor: ورابعا اشتماله على نزول قوله { ولما ضرب ابن مريم مثلا } الآية في الواقعة ولا ارتباط لمضمونها بها أصلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A popular version has Ibn al-Zibara argue that the verse says “what” is worshipped rather than “whom”; the author rejects the report’s attribution to the Prophet of the phrasing “I said this, not that,” and cites Ibn Hajar that it has no basis in the hadith books.
rows.anchor: لأني قلت وما تعبدون، وما لم يعقل، ولم أقل ومن تعبدون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further weak report says the Prophet answered that the righteous figures were not worshipped but the devils who ordered their worship; this argument would exclude idols too and make the verse apply only to devils, contrary to the report’s claim of universal scope.
rows.anchor: بل هم عبدوا الشياطين التي أمرتهم بذلك فأنزل الله { إن الذين سبقت لهم منا الحسنى }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report that 21:101 abrogated 21:98 is weak; if there is a relation, it is specification rather than abrogation.
rows.anchor: ووجه الضعف ظاهر ولو كان هناك شيء فهو التخصيص

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: In a report in al-Amali, the Prophet tells ʿAli that he and his Shiʿa will be secure at the Basin and on the Day of Greatest Terror, and says 21:101 and 70:35 were revealed concerning them.
rows.anchor: يا علي أنت وشيعتك على الحوض تسقون من أحببتم وتمنعون من كرهتم وأنتم الآمنون يوم الفزع الأكبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sacred symbols here are sacrificial camels marked by cutting the right side of the hump, ascribed to the Imams of the Prophet’s household; the context supports this through the benefits and the following mention of sacrificial camels.
rows.anchor: البدن التي تساق هديا وتشعر أي يشق سنامها من الجانب الأيمن ليعلم أنها هدي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alternative view that the symbols mean every sign set up for obedience does not fit the passage’s context.
rows.anchor: وقيل المراد بها جميع الأعلام المنصوبة للطاعة، والسياق لا يلائمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “it is from the piety of hearts” refers to honoring the sacred symbols, understood from the context, with the omitted noun replaced by its complement.
rows.anchor: فالضمير لتعظيم الشعائر المفهوم من الكلام ثم كأنه حذف المضاف وأقيم المضاف إليه مقامه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Piety is an inward moral restraint of the soul from God’s displeasure and forbidden acts, not bodily motions shared by obedience and sin or abstract labels derived from actions.
rows.anchor: حقيقة التقوى وهي التحرز والتجنب عن سخطه تعالى والتورع عن محارمه أمر معنوي يرجع إلى القلوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “their appointed term,” al-maḥill with kasra is a noun of time, and “in them” refers to the sacred symbols.
rows.anchor: المحل بكسر الحاء اسم زمان بمعنى وقت حلول الأجل وضمير { فيها } للشعائر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the symbols are sacrificial camels, their benefits are riding and drinking milk when needed until slaughter; their appointed end is at or on reaching the Kaʿba, as in the household Imams’ interpretation and the expression “an offering reaching the Kaʿba.”
rows.anchor: أن لكم في هذه الشعائر - وهي البدن - منافع من ركوب ظهرها وشرب ألبانها عنه الحاجة إلى أجل مسمى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the alternative reading that the symbols are pilgrimage rites, their benefits are commerce, and their endpoint is the Ancient House because circumambulation is the last rite.
rows.anchor: وأما على القول بكون المراد بالشعائر مناسك الحج فقيل المراد بالمنافع التجارة إلى أجل مسمى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Manسك is a verbal noun, temporal noun, or locative noun; because the verse says they remember God’s name, its apparent sense is a verbal noun for worship that includes slaughtering and offering sacrifice.
rows.anchor: وظاهر قوله { ليذكروا اسم الله } الخ أنه مصدر ميمي بمعنى العبادة وهي العبادة التي فيها ذبح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God prescribed sacrificial worship for each prior believing community, so Abraham’s followers are not the first community to receive sacrifice as a rite.
rows.anchor: لستم معشر أتباع إبراهيم أول أمة شرعت لهم التضحية وتقريب القربان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since God prescribed the rite for this community and earlier ones, their God is one; they must devote submission and sacrifice to Him alone rather than draw near to another.
rows.anchor: فأسلموا واستسلموا له بإخلاص عملكم له ولا تتقربوا في قرابينكم إلى غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first فاء (“for your God”) makes the consequence follow its cause, while the second (“so submit to Him”) makes the result follow its cause.
rows.anchor: فالفاء في { فإلهكم } لتفريع السبب على المسبب وفي قوله { فله أسلموا } لتفريع المسبب على السبب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise to give good news to the humble hints that one who submits sincerely to God in pilgrimage is among them; the next verse’s traits—reverent hearts, patience, prayer, and spending—fit the pilgrim.
rows.anchor: من أسلم لله في حجه مخلصا فهو من المخبتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-budn is the plural of badana, a large, fat she-camel, and becomes one of God’s sacred symbols by being designated as an offering.
rows.anchor: البدن بالضم فالسكون جمع بدنة بفتحتين وهي السمينة الضخمة من الإبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣawāff are standing camels with their forelegs and hind legs aligned and gathered, with their forelegs tied.
rows.anchor: ومعنى كونها صافة أن تكون قائمة قد صفت يداها ورجلاها وجمعت وقد ربطت يداها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wujūb means falling; the animals’ sides falling to the ground is a euphemism for their death, and eating from them lifts the prohibition and makes consumption permissible.
rows.anchor: والمراد بوجوب جنوبها سقوطها على الأرض على جنوبها وهو كناية عن موتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-qāniʿ is a poor person content with what is given, whether or not he asks.
rows.anchor: والقانع هو الفقير الذي يقنع بما أعطيه سواء سأل أم لا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-muʿtarr is a poor person who comes to someone seeking help.
rows.anchor: والمعتر هو الذي أتاك وقصدك من الفقراء

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله
rows.claim: Al-Majmaʿ reports from Abu ʿAbd Allah that the benefits are benefits of the afterlife, namely pardon and forgiveness; the author says naming one benefit does not exclude the general meaning.
rows.anchor: منافع الآخرة وهي العفو والمغفرة وهو المروي عن أبي عبد الله عليه السلام

rows.speaker: الرضا
rows.claim: In a letter to Muhammad ibn Sinan, al-Riḍā explains that pilgrimage is a visitation to God, seeking increase and repentance, beginning anew, spending wealth and tiring the body, restraining desires, and drawing near through worship and humility in heat, cold, safety, and fear.
rows.anchor: وعلة الحج الوفادة إلى الله عز وجل وطلب الزيادة والخروج من كل ما اقترف وليكون تائبا مما مضى

rows.speaker: الرضا
rows.claim: Al-Riḍā says pilgrimage benefits all people by directing hope and fear to God, softening hard hearts, ending forgetfulness and despair, renewing obligations, restraining corruption, and enabling commerce and the meeting of needs across regions for pilgrims and nonpilgrims.
rows.anchor: ومنه ترك قساوة القلب وجساؤة النفس ونسيان الذكر وانقطاع الرجاء والأمل، وتجديد الحقوق

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله
rows.claim: Abu al-Ṣabbāḥ al-Kinānī reports from Abu ʿAbd Allah that the “known days” are the Tashrīq days.
rows.anchor: قال هي أيام التشريق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other reports from al-Bāqir and al-Ṣādiq identify the known days as the first ten of Dhu al-Hijja, while some distinguish those as the known days and Tashrīq as the numbered days; the verse fits the latter Tashrīq interpretation better.
rows.anchor: والآية أشد ملاءمة لما يدل على أن المراد بالمعلومات أيام التشريق

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله
rows.claim: A report from Abu ʿAbd Allah glosses completing one’s untidiness as shaving and removing what is on the skin.
rows.anchor: قال هو الحلق وما في جلد الإنسان

rows.speaker: الرضا
rows.claim: Al-Riḍā explains completing one’s untidiness as trimming nails, removing dirt, and taking off the state of consecration.
rows.anchor: التفث تقليم الأظفار وطرح الوسخ وطرح الإحرام عنه

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله
rows.claim: Abu ʿAbd Allah identifies circumambulating the Ancient House with the women’s circumambulation (ṭawāf al-nisāʾ).
rows.anchor: قال هو طواف النساء

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Asked why the House is called the Ancient House, Abu Jaʿfar says it is a free, ancient house that no one has owned.
rows.anchor: هو بيت حر عتيق من الناس لم يملكه أحد

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله
rows.claim: In a report about Noah’s flood, Abu ʿAbd Allah says the House is called ancient because it was spared from the flood.
rows.anchor: وإنما سمي البيت العتيق لأنه أعتق من الغرق

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A report from ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr says the Prophet called it the Ancient House because God freed it from tyrants, so no tyrant ever prevailed over it; al-Tirmidhī graded the report good and al-Hākim sound.
rows.anchor: إنما سمى الله البيت العتيق لأن الله أعتقه من الجبابرة فلم يظهر عليه جبار قط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: History contradicts a literal claim that no tyrant ever prevailed: the House was destroyed by Ibn al-Zubayr, Husayn ibn Numayr for Yazid, al-Hajjaj for ʿAbd al-Malik, and the Qarmatians; the Prophet may have meant what had happened up to then, while the earlier report is unestablished.
rows.anchor: وقد خرب البيت ثم غيره عبد الله بن الزبير نفسه ثم الحصين بن نمير بأمر يزيد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that the Black Stone is part of the House because the Prophet circumambulated outside it, citing the command to circumambulate the Ancient House; the author notes similar reports from the household Imams.
rows.anchor: الحجر من البيت لأن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم طاف بالبيت من ورائه

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet tells the clan of ʿAbd Manāf not to prevent anyone from circumambulating the House or praying at any hour, day or night.
rows.anchor: لا تمنعوا أحدا طاف بهذا البيت وصلى أي ساعة شاء من ليل أو نهار

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: The author’s companions report that avoiding the filth of idols includes chess, backgammon, and other kinds of gambling.
rows.anchor: أن اللعب بالشطرنج والنرد وسائر أنواع القمار من ذلك

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: The author’s companions report that avoiding false speech includes singing and other distracting or frivolous speech.
rows.anchor: أنه يدخل فيه الغناء وسائر الأقوال الملهبة

rows.speaker: أيمن بن خزيم
rows.claim: Ayman ibn Khuzaym reports that the Prophet equated false testimony with associating partners with God and recited the command to avoid idol filth and false speech; the author notes this report also appears in al-Durr al-Manthūr.
rows.anchor: عدلت شهادة الزور بالشرك بالله ثم قرأ { فاجتنبوا الرجس من الأوثان واجتنبوا قول الزور }

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله
rows.claim: Abu ʿAbd Allah says one may ride a sacrificial camel without cruelty when in need, and milk it when needed without exhausting it.
rows.anchor: إن احتاج إلى ظهرها ركبها من غير عنف عليها وإن كان لها لبن حلبها حلابا لا ينهكها

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: A report from ʿAlī permits a man to ride his sacrificial camel in a reasonable manner; the author notes a similar report from the Prophet through Jābir.
rows.anchor: يركب الرجل بدنته بالمعروف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qummī commentary glosses submission and the glad tidings to the humble as referring to worshippers.
rows.anchor: قال العابدين

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله
rows.claim: Abu ʿAbd Allah says the camels stand in rows for slaughter with their forelegs tied between hoof and knee; their sides have fallen when they reach the ground.
rows.anchor: ذلك حين تصف للنحر تربط يديها ما بين الخف إلى الركبة، ووجوب جنوبها إذا وقعت على الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The chiefs’ claim that following a man like themselves would bring loss means that obeying someone with no superiority would destroy worldly happiness and freedom to enjoy life, which they regard as life’s only good, and amount to enslavement.
rows.anchor: وفي طاعة من لا فضل له عليكم رقيتكم وزوال حريتكم وهو الخسران

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disbelievers are likened to cattle, with a parallel at 7:170 and 47:12 describing disbelievers as eating as cattle eat.
rows.anchor: والذين كفروا يتمتعون ويأكلون كما تأكل الأنعام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their question about being brought out after becoming soil and bones refers to resurrection from graves for reckoning and recompense.
rows.anchor: للحساب والجزاء { هيهات هيهات لما توعدون }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Haihat means remote or impossible, and its repetition intensifies their declaration that the promised resurrection is far-fetched.
rows.anchor: وهيهات كلمة استبعاد وفي تكراره مبالغة في الاستبعاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We die and live” means that some people die and others are born in this world, continuing the cycle; the author mentions transmigration of souls as another possible sense, common among pagans, but says it fits the context poorly.
rows.anchor: أي يموت قوم منا في الدنيا ويحيا آخرون فيها لا نزال كذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “we die and live” could instead refer to transmigration, as souls leave one body at death and enter another human or nonhuman body; this was common among idolaters and sometimes called birth after birth.
rows.anchor: فإن التناسخ مذهب شائع عند الوثنيين وربما عبروا عنه بالولادة بعد الولادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the messenger a fabricator denies his prophetic claim after the leaders had already rejected monotheism and resurrection.
rows.anchor: يريدون به تكذيب دعواه الرسالة مع ما احتوت عليه دعوته وقد أنكروا التوحيد والمعاد قبل ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The leaders’ “we” may include themselves and the common people to avoid being suspected by the masses, or may refer only to the leaders, who state their disbelief so others will imitate them.
rows.anchor: ومرادهم بقولهم { نحن } أنفسهم وعامتهم أشركوا أنفسهم عامتهم لئلا يتهمهم العامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The chiefs’ arguments arise from their denial of monotheism, prophecy, and resurrection together with their indulgent worldly life.
rows.anchor: وقد نشأت هذه الأقاويل من اجتماع الصفات التي وصفهم الله به في أول الآيات وهي إنكار التوحيد والنبوة والمعاد والإتراف في الحياة الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening phrase places “of his people” before “who disbelieved,” unlike the previous story; this preserves the parallel order of “disbelieved,” “denied,” and “were indulged,” whereas placing it later would make the phrase too long.
rows.anchor: لأنه لو وقع بعد { الذين كفروا } اختل به ترتيب الجمل المتوالية { كفروا } { وكذبوا } { وأترفناهم }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s plea “My Lord, help me because they deny me” was already explained in the preceding story.
rows.anchor: تقدم تفسيرة في القصة السابقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s response promises the people’s regret as a euphemism for their annihilating punishment; “after little” means after a short interval, with mā intensifying the smallness, and the oath lam and emphatic nūn stressing that they will see it arrive.
rows.anchor: استجابة لدعوة الرسول وصيرورتهم نادمين كناية عن حلول عذاب الاستئصال بهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “the cry seized them in truth,” the preposition bi- may indicate accompaniment or causation; al-ḥaqq may stand for an omitted noun, meaning the true affair or decree.
rows.anchor: الباء في { بالحق } للمصاحبة وهو متعلق بقوله { فأخذتهم } أي أخذتهم الصيحة أخذا مصاحبا للحق
